mcqs.question: Why is hot-loading a plugin at runtime a materially harder problem than loading plugins at startup?
options: Hot-loading requires a completely different Plugin interface
It has to handle the plugin's classes already being in use, decide how in-flight calls to the old version finish, and often needs per-plugin classloader isolation to avoid symbol collisions
Hot-loading is actually simpler because there's no registry needed
It only matters for plugins written in a different programming language than the host
mcqs.explanation: Runtime replacement has to reconcile already-loaded classes, in-flight calls, and classloader isolation — none of which exist at startup when everything loads once before any request runs. It doesn't require a different interface, still needs a registry, and applies regardless of implementation language.

mcqs.question: In the execute() loop that calls each plugin, why is every plugin call wrapped in its own try/catch and timeout?
options: To make the loop run faster by parallelizing plugin calls
Because the PluginRegistry requires it to register a plugin
So one plugin throwing or hanging only removes that plugin's contribution for the request, without propagating a failure to the host or blocking other plugins
To automatically retry a failed plugin call a fixed number of times
mcqs.explanation: Per-call isolation contains a single plugin's failure or hang to just that plugin, protecting the host and every other plugin in the same request. It isn't about parallelism, registration, or automatic retries — none of those are what the try/catch and timeout are doing here.

mcqs.question: What's the actual architectural difference between a plugin system and the Strategy pattern?
options: Strategy always requires more interfaces than a plugin system
A plugin system never needs an interface at all
Strategy implementations must be discovered dynamically at runtime, exactly like plugins
Plugins are discovered dynamically and treated as an untrusted boundary, while Strategy implementations are wired by your own code at compile time with no such isolation needed
mcqs.explanation: The real difference is discovery and trust: Strategy choices are made by your own compiled code, while plugins are found dynamically and must be isolated since they're often unreviewed code. Both use an interface, and it's Strategy — not plugins — that's typically wired at compile time, not dynamically discovered.

mcqs.question: Why is handing a plugin a direct reference to the host's internal service objects a design mistake?
options: It erases the boundary between trusted host code and untrusted plugin code, letting a plugin call internals never meant for external use and coupling future refactors to plugin behavior
It makes the plugin interface violate the single responsibility principle
It's fine as long as the plugin is written by the same team as the host
It causes a compile error because internal objects can't be passed across a package boundary
mcqs.explanation: Direct access to internals removes the isolation a plugin boundary is supposed to provide, regardless of who authored the plugin, and it compiles just fine — the problem is architectural, not a language restriction. A curated PluginContext is the fix, not a same-team exception.
